newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO set to send more observers to Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO set to send more observers to Hebron.

text.p: Israel and the PLO were set on Monday to sign a deal to send more peacekeepers into violence-prone Hebron but an accord to extend Palestinian rule to the West Bank town remained elusive.

Israeli and Palestinian officials met in Jericho in the West Bank to sign an agreement that would increase the number of international observers stationed in Hebron to 210 from 30 once an overall self-rule deal was done.

U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross shuttled between Palestinian-ruled areas and Jerusalem trying yet again to bridge gaps between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"We have made a lot of progress. There is not a lot that separates the parties but there is not an agreement yet and we don't have an agreement until everything is resolved," Ross told reporters after meeting Netanyahu.
"And everything is not resolved," he added.

An overall accord would give Palestinians self-rule in most of Hebron, a volatile town of 100,000 Arabs and 400 Jews. Security issues and other concerns over the last 10 months have delayed the Israeli handover to Arafat's PLO.
Despite Ross's efforts, a Palestinian official accused the U.S. mediator of bias.

"I am astonished by Dennis Ross's statements which expressed his completely biased disposition," said Marwan Kanafani, an aide to Arafat, referring to statements attributed to Ross by the Israeli media.
The newspaper Haaretz quoted Ross and other U.S. officials as saying Netanyahu had been stretched "to the outer limits of his flexibility" and could make no further concessions.

"If he wants to continue his mediation between the two sides he has to adopt a just stand and an unbiased position. I think these statements harm the peace process," Kanafani told Israel Radio's Arabic service.
Ross was due to meet Arafat in self-ruled Bethlehem later.
Under the agreement on international observers, peacekeepers from Denmark, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey would join observers from Norway already stationed in the town.
Saeb Erekat, the chief PLO negotiator due to sign the deal on temporary observers, said on Sunday that the deal had been completed and would be signed in Jericho on Monday.

International observers went into Hebron under the 1995 Israel-PLO deal to maintain order, protect residents and monitor violations of the agreement. The new observers would arrive in Hebron only after Israel and the PLO sealed their Hebron deal.

PLO officials said the U.S. mediator had suggested a compromise to resolve a dispute over target dates for future redeployments in mostly rural areas in the West Bank which both sides say is the biggest obstacle to a deal.
Israel agreed in the 1995 deal with the PLO to withdraw from 80 percent of the town and committed to dates for further redeployments in the West Bank.

Netanyahu, who ousted the left-leaning government that signed the 1995 deal, is reluctant to complete the handover because of his opposition to swapping land for peace. But he says Israel must stick to its international commitments.
Netanyahu and Arafat met secretly under the cover of darkness early on Sunday but failed to break the deadlock.
